newsitem.title: SPAIN: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish Oct CPI rose 0.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish Oct CPI rose 0.1 pct.

text.p: Following is a selection of reactions to the Spanish Consumer Price Index which rose 0.1 percent in October month-on-month and 3.5 percent year-on-year.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected an 0.2 percent rise month-on-month and 3.6 percent gain year-on-year.
Core inflation rose 0.2 pct month-on-month and 3.2 percent year-on-year.
RICCARDO BARBIERI, ECONOMIST AT MORGAN STANLEY, LONDON:

"This is a very positive number. Especially the food prices are declining...This will allow the global index to decline even further in the coming months. Now the Bank of Spain's forecast for CPI at 3.4 percent at year end is more likely. With another good number, they can really decide a new rate cut of 25 basis points before year end."
CESAR MOLINAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH MADRID:

"The fiscal deficit is being brought down...but unless further efforts are made or lots of ingenuity applied to accounting, the outcome for 1997 will still be far away from the three percent target. A lot depends on how this criterion is applied."

Can the spread between Spanish bonos and German bunds, which hit an all-time low of 148 on Thursday, keep falling? Not unless markets price in early EMU entry, Molinas told Reuters Financial Television -- "which is something which despite all this Euro-optimism the markets haven't yet started to do."
VALENTIN FERNANDEZ, ECONOMIST AT CREDIT LYONNAIS, MADRID:
"It's a better figure than predicted to meet the inflation goal. Inflation at the end of this year could be around 3.3 percent (against an official target of 3.4 percent).
"Underlying inflation is coming under control, the trend is clearly downwards...but the Bank of Spain will not cut rates again before inflation falls below three percent."
XAVIER SEGURO, ECONOMIST AT CAIXA DE CATALUNYA: "The Bank of Spain has room to cut 25 basis points before the end of the year. Food prices have behaved better than predicted."
JUAN ANTONIO MIELGO, ECONOMIST, BANK OF AMERICA, MADRID:

"A good figure, especially underlying inflation which is more relevant for the Bank of Spain as well as for the markets. The best component is the figure for processed foods, where there doesn't seem to be an impact from the tax effect. I think the Bank of Spain will not do anything and that we will have to wait for another inflation figure and for amendments to the budget (to be out of the way in Parliament)."
"I don't think their (fiscal deficit) situation is any worse than (those of) France or Germany at this point."

"We think that Spain is not yet there (for EMU entry)...a 35 or 40 pct chance that they enter, but we cannot say that it is a likely event. I think it's going to be a remarkable rally in Spanish markets if it does enter, and it could happen quite suddenly."
